evidence.title: The Henry James Review
evidence.text: The Henry James Review is a triannual peer-reviewed academic journal established in 1979 and is the official publication of the Henry James Society.

evidence.title: The Henry James Review
evidence.text: It is dedicated to the scholarly, critical, and theoretical study of the American writer Henry James.

evidence.title: The Henry James Review
evidence.text: Each issue focuses on a specific theme of interest and seeks to promote understanding and study of James' contributions.

evidence.title: The Henry James Review
evidence.text: The journal is published by the Johns Hopkins University Press and the current editor-in-chief is Susan M. Griffin (University of Louisville).

evidence.title: Julie Rivkin
evidence.text: Julie H. Rivkin (born 1952) is an American literary critic and professor of English at Connecticut College since 1982.

evidence.title: Julie Rivkin
evidence.text: She is best known for her publications on literary theory and Henry James, and has published several works on both subjects.

evidence.title: Julie Rivkin
evidence.text: Rivkin received her B.A. and PhD from Yale University and is currently the Associate Dean of Faculty at Connecticut College, a member of the Modern Language Association, and Vice President of the Henry James Society.

evidence.title: Julie Rivkin
evidence.text: Her other specializations include American literature and gender studies (publisher of the "Henry James Review").

evidence.title: Simon Bent
evidence.text: Simon Bent is a British screenwriter and playwright, notable for work including BBC TV drama "" (2006), the screenplay for the feature film "Christie Malry's Own Double-Entry" (2000), and the Joe Orton biographical play "Prick Up Your Ears" based on John Lahr's book.

evidence.title: Joe Orton
evidence.text: John Kingsley "Joe" Orton (1 January 1933 – 9 August 1967) was an English playwright and author.

evidence.title: Joe Orton
evidence.text: His public career was short but prolific, lasting from 1964 until his death three years later.

evidence.title: Joe Orton
evidence.text: During this brief period he shocked, outraged, and amused audiences with his scandalous black comedies.

evidence.title: Joe Orton
evidence.text: The adjective "Ortonesque" is sometimes used to refer to work characterised by a similarly dark yet farcical cynicism.

evidence.title: What the Butler Saw (play)
evidence.text: What the Butler Saw is a farce written by the English playwright Joe Orton.

evidence.title: What the Butler Saw (play)
evidence.text: It was premièred at the Queen's Theatre in London on 5 March 1969.

evidence.title: What the Butler Saw (play)
evidence.text: It was Orton's final play and the second to be performed after his death, following "Funeral Games" in 1968.

evidence.title: Prick Up Your Ears
evidence.text: Prick Up Your Ears is a 1987 British film, directed by Stephen Frears, about the playwright Joe Orton and his lover Kenneth Halliwell.

evidence.title: Prick Up Your Ears
evidence.text: The screenplay was written by Alan Bennett, based on the biography by John Lahr.

evidence.title: Prick Up Your Ears
evidence.text: The film stars Gary Oldman as Orton, Alfred Molina as Halliwell, Wallace Shawn as Lahr and Vanessa Redgrave as Peggy Ramsay.

evidence.title: Henry James
evidence.text: Henry James, OM ((1843--)15 1843 – (1916--)28 1916 ) was an American author regarded as a key transitional figure between literary realism and literary modernism, and is considered by many to be among the greatest novelists in the English language.

evidence.title: Henry James
evidence.text: He was the son of Henry James, Sr. and the brother of renowned philosopher and psychologist William James and diarist Alice James.

evidence.title: The Ruffian on the Stair
evidence.text: The Ruffian On the Stair is a play by British playwright Joe Orton which was first broadcast on BBC Radio in August 1964.

evidence.title: The Ruffian on the Stair
evidence.text: It is an unsympathetic yet comedic one-act portrayal of working class England, as played out by a couple and a mysterious young man who toys with their lives.

evidence.title: The Ruffian on the Stair
evidence.text: It was based on "The Boy Hairdresser", a novel by Orton and his lover Kenneth Halliwell.

evidence.title: The Ruffian on the Stair
evidence.text: The title and play are based on a few lines from poet and dramatist William Ernest Henley: "Madam Life's a piece in bloom, / Death goes dogging everywhere: / She's the tenant of the room, / He's the ruffian on the stair."

evidence.title: The Ruffian on the Stair
evidence.text: "Ruffian" is not as renowned as other works such as "Loot" and "What the Butler Saw", but it is still staged on occasion.

evidence.title: Plain Clothes Theatre Productions
evidence.text: Plain Clothes Theatre Productions is a Bristol-based theatre company producing contemporary plays from around the globe.

evidence.title: Plain Clothes Theatre Productions
evidence.text: Formed in 2003 by artistic director Sam Berger, the company has produced work in London, Bristol, Cheltenham, Toronto and Vancouver.

evidence.title: Plain Clothes Theatre Productions
evidence.text: Their work has included plays by Joe Orton, Laura Wade and David Mamet, and their style is based around the teachings of American acting coach Sanford Meisner.

evidence.title: Prick Up Your Ears (play)
evidence.text: Prick Up Your Ears is a play by Simon Bent, based on the life of playwright Joe Orton.

evidence.title: Prick Up Your Ears (play)
evidence.text: Produced by Sonia Friedman it opened at the Comedy Theatre in London's West End on 30 September 2009 following previews from 17 September.

evidence.title: Prick Up Your Ears (play)
evidence.text: It starred Chris New as Joe Orton and Matt Lucas as Orton's lover and murderer, Kenneth Halliwell.
